Seminar Title:

Feminist Re-Mapping through Food: Intergenerational Negotiations, Female Agency and Self-Articulation in Contemporary Indian Diasporic Fiction

Seminar Type:

Synopsis Seminar

Department:

Humanities and Social Sciences

Speaker Name:

Shraddha Chatterjee ( Rollno : 517hs3008)

Speaker Type:

Student

Venue:

HS Seminar Room (MN436)

Date and Time:

17 Nov 2026 5.15pm

Contact:

Seemita Mohanty

Abstract:

The kitchen has always been construed as a gendered space. However, diasporic foodways have long defied the traditional norms of the kitchen as a confinement. This is evident in the ways diasporic women have been recently reframing the kitchen as a space for redefining their identities. This study contributes to the scholarship at the intersection of food, gender and diaspora by investigating domestic culinary spaces as locations for cultural negotiations and feminist self-articulation. It offers fresh perspectives on diasporic foodways by viewing the kitchen not merely as a space of nostalgia, as existing food scholarship has illustrated, but also as a safe space of renewed significance. Indian diaspora proves to be one of the most diverse diasporas in the world, where the cultural practices of each diasporic household are distinct from one another. This is chiefly due to the dynamic nature of the country, wherein every state has its own language, culture and culinary history. Such differences become particularly significant as the culinary traditions also vary from one state to another. The present study analyses such culinary negotiations in three Indian diasporic novels, chiefly centring on women. Grounded in feminist studies and food criticism, the study offers fresh perspectives on diasporic foodways through a comparative close reading of three texts: Amulya Malladi&rsquos Serving Crazy with Curry (2004), Amit Majmudar&rsquos The Abundance (2013) and Sandeepa Mukherjee Datta&rsquos Those Delicious Letters (2020). The analysis is further strengthened by interviews conducted with Sandeepa Mukherjee Datta and Amit Majmudar, which offer additional insights into the interiority of their female characters, provide interpretive cues and offer circumstantial insights. It examines the role of the kitchen in mediating intergenerational relationships between immigrant mothers and their second-generation daughters, with the connections extending to both consanguineal and affinal ties. The study then scrutinises how culinary techniques, such as improvisation and adaptation, along with the gatekeeping of authentic cooking within the diaspora, function as modes of preserving techniques while upholding maternal culinary pedagogy as a chief mode of knowledge transmission. Finally, it considers the diverse trajectories through which culinary practices move beyond commonplace domestic contexts to become forms of cultural production and feminist self-articulation. It does so by exploring three means through which cooking acquires salience: the pursuit of professional aspiration, culinary authorship and the documentation of recipes while safeguarding them against commercialisation. It further shows that all three modes do not represent the outcome of individual accomplishments, but they highlight the different ways agency is exercised, circulated and valued. It foregrounds that the diasporic kitchen is both a complex and a dynamic space in which women question gendered expectations, yet celebrate cultural continuity while sustaining traditional expectations in their own ways without renouncing them completely. Thus, this study elucidates how cooking enables Indian diasporic women to pursue their feminine voice by foregrounding the kitchen as a dynamic space of narrative agency in the diasporic context. It offers a feminist re-evaluation of the kitchen as a site of meaning-making, enriching the literary representation of domesticity and intergenerational intimacy among diasporic women.
